title: Slander
hookLine: spreading falsehood that harms a name

cards: Who started it? By the fourth telling, nobody can say. A parent at school pickup sees a for-sale sign on a family's lawn and wonders aloud whether they're in trouble with money.
The next parent repeats it as a fact. By Friday the family is losing the house. None of it happened.

They're moving to be closer to a grandmother who needs help. But the story has a life of its own, and the true version never travels as fast. Jewish teaching has a separate, heavier name for harmful speech that's false.

teach.b: Motzi shem ra. Word for word, bringing out a bad name. Turn it four ways.

First, it's the Torah's own phrase. In Deuteronomy a man turns against his new wife and invents an accusation against her, and the text says he "hath brought up an evil name" on her. The law takes her side.
The lie is treated as an injury, and he pays for it. A name, in this picture, can be wounded. Second, where it sits.
The Chafetz Chaim, among other teachers, draws a line.
Lashon hara is a hurtful thing that's true. Motzi shem ra is a hurtful thing that's false. The first is already forbidden; the second adds a lie to the harm, and tradition counts it heavier.

teach.h: NO FALSE WITNESS, EVEN AT HOME.
teach.b: Third, the commandment behind it: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." Some hear that only in a courtroom.
The teachers of speech hear it at the kitchen table too, because a rumor is testimony with no judge to check it. Fourth, the small versions. A guess passed along as fact.
A detail dropped that would have changed the story. "I heard she..." with nothing behind it. And because a false story keeps moving, Jewish teaching on repentance asks for more than going quiet.
It asks for repair: going back, as far as you can reach, and setting it straight.
That's harder than silence. It's also the one thing that goes after the story once it has left.

how: Jewish teaching on speech distinguishes lashon hara, hurtful truth, from motzi shem ra, hurtful falsehood; repentance for it is understood to include repairing the harm, not only stopping.

o: a false story that damages someone's name
a nickname given to tease or mock someone
an insult said straight to a person's face

games.q: motzi shem ra — tap the pairs.
p: he brought up an evil name
going back to set it straight

s: motzi shem ra is the same as lashon hara
lashon hara is hurtful and true. motzi shem ra is hurtful and false, and tradition counts it heavier.
the phrase comes from the Torah itself
Deuteronomy says the husband "hath brought up an evil name" on his wife.
once you stop spreading a false story, you're done
Jewish teaching on repentance asks for repair: going back and setting it straight.

games.q: you passed along a story about a coworker last week. today you learn it was false. what do you do?
o: say nothing more and let it fade.
go back to the people who heard it from you and set it straight.
start a new story to cover the old one.
games.why: Jewish teaching on repentance asks for repair: a false story keeps moving, so going quiet isn't enough.

practice: Look back for one thing you said or let stand that was wrong about someone, maybe a guess about why a friend canceled, and see whoever heard it from you.
Find the plain sentence that would set it straight, I said that, and I was wrong, and say it once, silently.
If nothing comes to mind, picture a false story going around and the one true sentence that could replace it; if you pray, you can ask for the nerve to say it out loud.

wordCard.voice: Motzi shem ra. Bringing out a bad name: harmful speech that is also false. The phrase comes from Deuteronomy itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing out a bad name. The wording echoes Deuteronomy 22.

carryVoice: Your line: no false names. Repair is harder than silence, and it reaches further. Gently, until tomorrow.
